adults.title: Helping the Lord Keep His Promise
adults.big_idea: The Lord keeps His promise to be with us in our trials, through the Holy Ghost and through faithful disciples, and He trusts us to be those disciples for others.
adults.objective: Learners will recognize one way the Lord has kept His promise to be with them and will choose one person to reach out to this week as His helper.
prepare: Read President Eyring's talk, marking paragraphs 5–8 (his mother's answer), 11–13 (the hospital) and 16–21 (four ways to help).
Write on the board: The promise is not for the removal of challenges.
Bring slips of paper and pens, and four cards labeled with the paragraph numbers 16, 17–18, 19–20 and 21.
Pray to know who in the class may be carrying something heavy today.

segments.name: A promise sung to us
steps: After the prayer, sing or read together the verse of “How Firm a Foundation” that President Eyring quoted (paragraph 4 of the talk). Explain that the choir had just sung this hymn and that he said its words come from Isaiah 41.
Tell the class his message in one line: the promises in that hymn are true.
Ask the first question and give a full minute of silence before anyone answers. Take two or three brief responses.
questions: Which phrase in this verse do you most need to be true this week? You do not have to say why.

segments.name: What the promise is, and what it is not
steps: Point to the sentence on the board. Invite someone to read paragraphs 5–7: the boy who asked his mother why life is so hard, her answer, and what he realized years later about her own trials.
Have everyone read Isaiah 41:10 silently and count what the Lord says He will do. List the answers on the board.
Read paragraph 8 aloud. Ask the questions below. Let people answer each other; you do not need to comment on every reply.
If it helps the discussion, share Elder Hathaway's sentence about grace as an enabling power.
questions: President Eyring's mother said life is a test while she was living through one. What does that add to her answer?
What is different about praying for a trial to end and praying to feel the Lord with you in it? When have you needed each?
According to paragraph 8, why does a loving God allow the test to be hard?

segments.name: Evidence from a hospital room
steps: Retell paragraphs 11–12 simply: in her last days his mother was bedridden; the only picture on her bedroom wall was of the Savior, where she could see it from her bed. His father had a cot placed beside her in the hospital room so he could help her at once during the nights. After she died, his father walked the ward to thank and shake the hand of every nurse who had helped her.
Read President Kimball's statement from paragraph 13, and President Eyring's sentence that the Lord sends faithful disciples to help Him keep His promise.
Ask learners to turn to one person and share for two minutes.
questions: Who are the disciples in this story? What did each one do?
When has the Lord's help reached you through another person? What did that person actually do?

segments.name: Four ways we already help
steps: Explain that President Eyring used the rest of his message to thank those who serve this way and to encourage others to join. Divide into four groups and hand out the cards: paragraph 16 (praying to know whom to help), 17–18 (a discouraged missionary), 19–20 (those serving in callings), 21 with Mosiah 18:8–9 (comforting those who plead for comfort).
Give groups four minutes to find two things: what the helper does, and what the person helped comes to know about the Lord.
Have each group report in thirty seconds. Write the second answers on the board; they will be nearly the same: the Lord knows me and loves me.
Check for understanding by asking the question below.
questions: How small are the acts President Eyring describes? Why do you think he chose such small ones?

segments.name: A face or a name
steps: Read paragraph 22 aloud. Note the two parts: the Lord will comfort all who try to follow Him, and He offers us the blessing and trust of helping.

Hand out slips of paper. Allow two minutes of silence. Invite each person to pray silently and write any face or name that comes to mind, and one simple thing to do for that person within the next few days.

Bear your testimony that the Savior keeps His promises. Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking what happened when they reached out, and what they noticed about the Lord's care for that person.
Close with the last verse of “How Firm a Foundation” if time allows.

key_quotes.text: It is important to realize that the promise is not for the removal of challenges.
the Lord sends faithful disciples to help Him keep His promise to succor others in their distress
That you felt prompted to reach out to them was evidence to them that the Lord knew and loved them.

We know that the Lord will comfort all of those who try to follow Him. And He offers us the great blessing and trust to help Him keep His promise to succor Heavenly Father’s children in their tests along their mortal journey toward home.

scriptures.use: Read silently in the second segment; count and list on the board what the Lord says He will do. Notice that removing the trial is not on the list.
The fourth group reads it with paragraph 21 and names what those who want to be called His people are willing to do for one another.
Optional in the third segment: read with paragraph 9 and ask what it means that the Savior carried our sorrows, not only understood them.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball
aligned_quotes.text: God does notice us, and he watches over us. But it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Hathaway
aligned_quotes.text: This grace does not remove the pain and difficulty of affliction; it is an enabling power

takeaways: The Lord's promise is to be with us and strengthen us, not to remove every challenge.
He keeps that promise through the Holy Ghost and, usually, through another person.
A prompting to reach out to someone is the Lord's trust in me and His love for them.
act: Each morning this week, pray to know whom the Lord would have you help, and act on the first face or name that comes.
Speak to a missionary, in person or by message, and tell them one specific thing you appreciate about their service.
Thank someone serving in a calling in your ward or branch and tell them how their service has blessed you.
Sit with, call or visit one person who is mourning or worn down. Listen more than you speak.
adapt: At home or with fewer than six people: skip the groups. Read paragraphs 16–21 together, pausing after each way to ask who comes to mind.
Large class: keep the four paragraph assignments but have people work with the two or three sitting nearest them, and take only one report for each paragraph.
Short on time: shorten the hospital-room segment to the story and President Kimball's words, and protect the last five minutes of silent writing.

youth.title: Why Is Life So Hard?
youth.big_idea: Life is meant to be a test, but the Savior promises to be with us in it, and He often sends help through people, including us.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain what the Lord promises in Isaiah 41:10 and will send or say one real word of encouragement to someone who needs it.
prepare: Read President Eyring's talk, especially paragraphs 5–10 and 16–20.
Bring small cards or scraps of paper, pens, and a timer (a phone works).
Bring a backpack with four or five heavy books in it.
Ask youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app ready.

segments.name: Sixty seconds, no names
steps: As youth arrive, hand each a card. Start the timer: they have sixty seconds to write, without their name, one thing that makes life hard for people their age.
Collect the cards, shuffle them, and read five or six aloud without comment.
Say that today's talk starts with a boy who asked his mother the same kind of question.

segments.name: Hal's question
steps: Have one youth read the boy's question in paragraph 5 and another read his mother's answer in paragraph 6. Explain that the boy was President Eyring.
Ask the first question below. Let them be honest; do not rush to fix their answers.
Read paragraph 7 together: his mother was going through serious, lifelong health trials of her own when she said it. Ask the second question.
Read paragraphs 8 and 10. Ask the third question and write their answers on the board.
questions: If you asked that question and got that answer, how would you feel? Helped, annoyed, something else?
Does it change anything to know she was living through hard things herself when she said it?
President Eyring says everyone's trials are different but the test is the same. In your own words, what is being tested?

segments.name: Promise hunt
steps: Split into two or three teams. Everyone opens Isaiah 41:10. Give ninety seconds: each team lists every promise the Lord makes in that one verse. The longest correct list wins.
Have the winning team read its list. Then ask all teams to look once more for what the verse does not promise.
Read the first sentences of paragraph 5 and the line from Elder Hathaway about grace as an enabling power.
Read paragraph 9 aloud, slowly. Invite youth to mark it.
questions: Which would you choose if you could pick only one: a problem removed, or the Lord with you in it? Why?
What difference does it make that the Savior knows you perfectly and knows your heart?

segments.name: The backpack
steps: Ask a volunteer to hold the backpack of books straight out in front with both arms while you tell the story. Tell them to lower it whenever they need to.

Tell paragraphs 11–12 in your own words: when President Eyring's mother was bedridden at the end of her life, the only picture on her bedroom wall was of the Savior. His father had a cot put beside her in the hospital room so he could help her during the nights, and after she died he thanked and shook the hand of every nurse who had helped her.
Midway, have a second youth step in and hold the pack from underneath. Ask the volunteer what changed. The weight is still there; the help is what is new.
Read President Kimball's words from paragraph 13.
questions: Who has been the person holding up the pack for you?

segments.name: A few seconds
steps: Read paragraph 18 and the first three sentences of paragraph 16. Point out how small these acts are: a few seconds, a smile, simple attention.

In pairs, give each pair one person to encourage: a missionary who is discouraged, a leader or teacher in a calling, or someone your age who is having a hard time. They have three minutes to write on a phone or card the exact words they would say or send. It must sound like them and be something they would really send.
Invite three pairs to read theirs. Let the group pick the one that would mean the most to receive, and say why.
questions: What makes a message like this feel real instead of awkward?

segments.name: Your move
steps: Give one minute of silence. Invite each youth to pray silently and ask who needs to hear from them. If a face or a name comes, write it down.
Challenge them to send or say their message within twenty-four hours, and to pray each day this week to notice one more person.
Read paragraph 22 and bear a short testimony that the Savior is with them in what is hard and that He trusts them to help.
Tell them you will ask next week: who did you reach out to, and what happened?

key_quotes.text: Hal, of course it’s hard. It’s supposed to be. Life is a test.
He knows you perfectly. He knows your heart.
Even your simple attention was a comfort.
Your kindness to them, even for a few seconds, or simply a warm smile can be a strengthening of their faith that the Lord is watching over them.

scriptures.use: Team race in the third segment: list every promise the Lord makes in the verse, then look for what it does not promise.
Before the pairs write their messages, read it and ask which phrase describes what they are about to do.
Optional with paragraph 9: read silently and find why the Savior is able to know how to help us.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball
aligned_quotes.text: God does notice us, and he watches over us. But it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Hathaway
aligned_quotes.text: This grace does not remove the pain and difficulty of affliction; it is an enabling power

takeaways: Life is hard on purpose; it is a test, and hard does not mean I am doing it wrong.
The Savior knows me perfectly and promises to be with me and strengthen me.
A few seconds of my kindness can help someone believe the Lord is watching over them.
act: Within twenty-four hours, send or say the encouraging message you wrote today.
Pray each morning this week to notice one person who needs help, and act on the first face or name that comes.
Greet the missionaries or a ward leader by name on Sunday and thank them for one specific thing.
Put Isaiah 41:10 where you will see it, such as your lock screen, and read it when the week gets hard.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: skip teams. List the promises in Isaiah 41:10 together and write one message each.
Large class: run the promise hunt in rows and have pairs trade messages with the pair beside them instead of reading aloud.
No backpack: have the volunteer hold two hymnbooks at arm's length instead.

children.title: Jesus Is with Me, and I Can Be His Helper
children.big_idea: Jesus is with me when things are hard, and He sends helpers. I can be one of His helpers.
children.objective: Children will be able to say the words “Fear not, I am with thee” and name one kind thing they will do to help someone this week.
prepare: Bring a picture of the Savior.
Bring a blanket and four or five books.
Bring paper and crayons for each child, and a soft ball.
Read paragraphs 5–6, 11–13 and 16–18 of President Eyring's talk so you can tell the story in your own simple words.

segments.name: Welcome and song
steps: Invite a child to pray. Sing the song I'm Trying to Be like Jesus.
Hold up the picture of the Savior. Ask the question below and let several children answer.
Tell them: today we will learn a promise from Jesus.
questions: Who has helped you when something was hard? What did they do?

segments.name: Learn the promise with actions
steps: Explain that President Eyring taught us a promise from the scriptures and from a hymn: “Fear not, I am with thee.” Tell the children that thee means you.
Teach actions. Fear not: shake your head and hold your hands out, palms forward. I am: point up. With thee: hug yourself.
Say it together three times: once in a whisper, once in a normal voice, once standing tall.
Tell the children that whenever you hold up the picture of the Savior today, everyone says the promise with the actions.

segments.name: The story of Hal and his mother
steps: Tell the story simply. When President Eyring was a little boy called Hal, he asked his mother why life is so hard. She smiled and told him it is supposed to be hard, because life is a test. His mother was sick for much of her life, but she knew Jesus was with her.

Continue: when she was very sick and had to stay in bed, she kept one picture on her wall where she could see it. Ask the children to guess whose picture. Hold up the picture of the Savior and say the promise together.

Continue: Hal's father slept on a little bed right beside her in the hospital so he could help her in the night. Nurses helped her too. Later, his father found every nurse, shook each one's hand and said thank you.
Have the children stand, shake hands with two others and say thank you, the way his father did.
questions: Who were the helpers in this story?

segments.name: The heavy blanket
steps: Lay the blanket on the floor and put the books in the middle. Ask one child to try lifting it by one corner. It sags and the books slide.
Ask who could help. Have three more children each take a corner and lift together, slowly. Let other children take turns.
Point out that the books are still heavy, but with helpers the load can be carried. Explain that Jesus is with us, and He sends helpers too.
Hold up the picture of the Savior. Say the promise together.
questions: How did it feel when your friends took the other corners?

segments.name: My helping hand
steps: Give each child paper and a crayon. Help them trace one hand.
Say that President Eyring taught that even a warm smile or a few seconds of kindness can help someone know that Jesus is watching over them.
Inside the hand, each child draws one kind thing they can do this week: smile at someone, say thank you to a teacher, pray for someone, sit by someone who is alone, say hello to the missionaries.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about their drawing.

segments.name: Helper ball
steps: Stand or sit in a circle. Say the first half of this sentence and roll or toss the ball to a child, who finishes it: I can be a helper for Jesus by ...
The child names one way to help, then sends the ball to someone who has not had a turn. Keep going until everyone has had the ball.
If a child is stuck, let them hold up their hand drawing and tell what is on it.

segments.name: Remember and go
steps: Hold up the picture of the Savior one last time. Say the promise together with the actions.
Bear a short testimony: Jesus knows you. He is with you when things are hard. He is glad when you help.
Invite the children to take their hand drawing home and do the kind thing they drew. Tell them that next week you will ask what they did.
Close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: Fear not, I am with thee; oh, be not dismayed,
He knows you perfectly. He knows your heart.
Even your simple attention was a comfort.

scriptures.use: Show the children where the promise is found. An older child reads the verse aloud while the others do the actions when they hear the words they learned.
After the blanket activity, an older child reads verse 8 aloud. Ask what the people were willing to do with one another's burdens.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball
aligned_quotes.text: God does notice us, and he watches over us.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Rasband
aligned_quotes.text: Love is being there with arms outstretched and a cheerful countenance.

takeaways: Jesus is with me when things are hard.
I can be a helper for Jesus.
act: Do the kind thing you drew inside your helping hand.
Say thank you to someone who helps you, such as a teacher, a leader or a nurse.
Pray for someone who is having a hard time.
Say the promise with the actions when you feel afraid or sad.
music: I'm Trying to Be like Jesus

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: tell the story in four or five sentences and repeat the promise with actions after each part. Use only one book on the blanket and let every child have a turn at a corner. Trace hands for them and let them simply color; ask each child to tell you one kind thing. Roll the ball on the floor instead of tossing it, and accept a one-word answer such as smile or hug.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have them find and read Isaiah 41:10 and Mosiah 18:8 aloud. Ask a harder question: Jesus promised to be with us, not to take every hard thing away. Why might that be better? Read Elder Rasband's sentence and ask what a cheerful countenance looks like. Let an older child lead the blanket activity or the ball game, and have them write the name of someone they will help inside their hand.
